sections.h2: Villages, hamlets and your mailing address
sections.html:
The Town of Oyster Bay is the easternmost of Nassau County's three towns and spans from the Long Island Sound shore to the South Shore, roughly 169.5 square miles with about 38 percent of that water. Inside it are 18 villages and 18 hamlets, served by 20 post offices and 30 ZIP codes. Post office names match those places, but the boundaries usually do not, so the town on your mailing address may not be the village or hamlet your lot sits in.

Begin with the section, block and lot printed on your tax bill, then ask the town whether your house is inside a village. That answer decides which offices handle permits and local rules for your property.

The town had 301,115 residents in July 2025, living in 100,559 households. About 89.1 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the typical owned home is valued at $708,600, and median rent is $2,572 a month. Owners with a mortgage have a median monthly cost of $3,910, and median household income is $160,126. Since 93.3 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, listings are not plentiful.

With owners in nearly nine of ten homes, most sellers have a mortgage to pay off. Request a payoff figure from your lender early so the number is ready when you take an offer.

sections.h2: Receiver of Taxes: bills, due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Two bills come each year, a school bill mailed in October and a general bill mailed in January, and each splits into halves. Owners with an escrow account have the bills sent to their lender.

Oyster Bay tax payment windows
BillDuePaid without penalty through
General tax, first halfJanuary 1February 10
General tax, second halfJuly 1August 10
School tax, first halfOctober 1November 10
School tax, second halfApril 1May 10

A late payment picks up a 1 percent monthly penalty, counted back to the original due date. Collection closes on May 31 for school bills and August 31 for general bills, and after that unpaid amounts move to the Nassau County Treasurer. The word Arrears in the upper left corner of a bill means that has happened. Payments are taken at Town Hall North in Oyster Bay and Town Hall South in Massapequa, by mail and online. Only a United States Postal Service postmark proves a mailed payment arrived on time.

A new owner should write to the Receiver so the next bill goes to the right address. Banks, title companies and attorneys paying on someone else's behalf owe a $10 duplicate bill fee with each payment, a point to raise when the closing statement is drafted.

Complaints go to Nassau County, and the deadline is March 1. The county's Assessment Review Commission meets through the year but accepts complaints only until that date. Ask the commission for forms and instructions. This is a different calendar from the spring Grievance Day that town boards hold in much of New York.

Home improvements can change an assessment through the Nassau County Department of Assessment in Mineola. If you added a dormer, finished a basement or built a deck, a buyer's tax bill may end up different from yours, so ask the county for the figure on file and compare it with the work you did.

sections.h2: What the Nassau County Clerk requires to record a deed
sections.html:
The clerk's office is at 240 Old Country Road in Mineola. Its Land Recording Guide puts the property's section, block and lot first. A missing or invalid number is the most common reason for rejection, and the clerk does not check it, so copy it from the current county tax bill.

  • Documents must be notarized, legible and signed in original ink, with party names matching exactly between the heading and the acknowledgment.
  • Post office boxes are not accepted as addresses.
  • Transfer tax goes by certified check; recording fees can go by personal check or Visa or MasterCard.
  • Present documents at least an hour before the closing.
  • Three approved companies offer e-recording, which title firms and attorneys usually use.

Forms TP-584 and RP-5217 travel with the deed. A nonresident seller who owes estimated income tax on the gain files Form IT-2663 and pays that tax to the recording officer when the deed is filed. Confirm current fees on the clerk's website before the closing.

sections.h2: Transfer tax for an Oyster Bay seller
sections.html:
New York charges two dollars on every $500 of price, counting a partial $500 as whole, and the seller carries that by default. Ask the Nassau County Clerk whether any county or local charge also applies to your deed, since the state rate is only the statewide piece.

At $1 million or more for a residence, a 1 percent mansion tax falls on the buyer. Read the contract anyway, since the parties may shift the base tax, and the state makes buyer and seller jointly liable when the tax goes unpaid.

An owner of a house with up to four units must sign the state's seller form and deliver it ahead of the buyer's contract signature. With a long Sound and bay shoreline, the flood section gets close reading. It asks about FEMA floodplain and flood hazard zones, flood insurance, elevation certificates, earlier flood claims, sump pumps and water entering the building from storm surge or tidal inundation.

Building permits run through the town's Department of Planning and Development, which posts application forms at oysterbaytown.com/building. Before listing, write down past work such as pools, fences, generators and solar panels and confirm each was permitted. The form also asks about certificates of occupancy, and an unclosed permit is easier to fix before a contract than after.

sections.h2: When does a cash purchase make sense for an Oyster Bay house?
sections.html:
It fits when time matters more than the top price. With no buyer lender involved, the schedule rests on payoffs, the tax steps above and recording in Mineola. Have your last tax receipt, your deed and any open permit paperwork on the table before you ask anyone for a number.

Ask for the offer in writing and find out who pays each closing cost. Confirm the buyer's plan for transfer tax, since the state makes buyer and seller jointly responsible if it is left unpaid. If the sale is a quick one, call the Receiver of Taxes for a current balance so that no school or general bill is waiting in arrears when the deed is delivered.

faqs.q: When is the first half of Oyster Bay's general tax due?
faqs.a: January 1, payable without penalty through February 10. The second half is due July 1 and payable through August 10. The school bill keeps its own calendar, with October 1 and April 1 due dates.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss an Oyster Bay tax deadline?
faqs.a: A 1 percent monthly penalty accrues, counted from the original due date. After May 31 for school bills and August 31 for general bills, the unpaid balance is payable to the Nassau County Treasurer instead of the Receiver of Taxes.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to challenge an Oyster Bay assessment?
faqs.a: March 1. Nassau County's Assessment Review Commission accepts complaints through that date, and the commission can give you the forms.

faqs.q: Which number must appear on a Nassau County deed?
faqs.a: The section, block and lot, plus a unit number for a condominium. Copy it from the current tax bill and put it on the first page. Mistakes here cause more rejected filings than any other error.

faqs.q: Who pays the mansion tax on an Oyster Bay house that sells for $1 million or more?
faqs.a: The buyer. The mansion tax is 1 percent of the price on a residence sold at $1 million or more, and the seller owes it only if the buyer fails to pay. The base transfer tax of $2 per $500 is the seller's by default.
